author: Booggers
quote: I waited over a decade for this game and I never thought the biggest issue with a new GTA would be how painfully bad and sanitized the story is. Rockstar completely lost the edge that made this franchise legendary in the first place. Instead of sharp satire that used to make fun of everyone equally, we got a safe, preachy, overly woke script that feels like it was approved by a corporate HR department. The jokes fall completely flat, the writing is scared to actually offend anyone, and the plot drags on with zero real stakes. It honestly does not even feel like a real Grand Theft Auto game **** worst part by far is the main cast. The male lead is a complete joke, totally bland, passive, and treated like a doormat for basically the entire campaign. He feels like a nobody compared to the female protagonist, who is written like the most cliché modern girlboss imaginable. She is always right, always effortlessly tough, bosses everyone around without ever facing real pushback, while he just stands there taking orders and looking incompetent. There is zero real chemistry between them, and by the halfway point I could not care less what happened to either of **** does not get any better with the supporting cast either, because there is not a single memorable or genuinely interesting character in this entire game. Previous GTA titles gave us iconic characters and unforgettable dialogue, while everyone here feels flat, generic, and completely forgettable. Every cutscene feels like a chore to sit through. Combine that with rough performance on PS5 and the same outdated mission structure, and you get the biggest gaming letdown in years. The old Rockstar is clearly gone, and pretty graphics cannot save a game with no soul.

author: Booggers
quote: After years of hype and promises of a “next-gen open world experience,” Crimson Desert ends up being a classic case **** trying to do everything… and not doing anything particularly well. The biggest issue is how chaotic it feels. The game throws a massive number of systems, mechanics, and activities at you, but never manages to tie them together in a meaningful way. Within the first few hours, it already feels bloated and unfocused. Instead of a living, immersive world, you get something that feels like messy design without clear direction. The usability is another major problem: clunky interface and inventory management, lack of basic quality-of-life features, questionable design choices (like inconsistent enemy behavior and awkward looting systems)Technically, it’s also uneven. Performance can be unstable depending on the platform, with noticeable frame drops and optimization issues. Visually, it looks impressive at times, but inconsistent overall. What’s most disappointing is that after such a long development cycle and massive ambition, the final result feels… average. Not terrible, but far from what was promised or expected. Crimson Desert is a textbook example of style over substance. Big world, lots of ideas, but not enough polish. If you were expecting a genre-defining RPG, lower your expectations significantly.

author: Booggers
quote: Overwatch isn’t just a shooter it’s a masterclass in team-based game design. From the moment you step into a match, it’s clear that every element has been carefully crafted. The heroes are diverse, both in gameplay and personality, each offering unique abilities that fundamentally change how matches unfold. Whether you’re coordinating pushes as a tank, clutch-healing as a support, or carrying fights as a damage dealer, every role feels impactful and **** gameplay is incredibly polished. Movement is fluid, abilities are responsive, and the gunplay strikes a perfect balance between accessibility and depth. Team coordination is at the heart of the experience, rewarding communication, strategy, and adaptability over raw mechanical skill alone.What truly elevates Overwatch is its character design and world-building. Each hero feels alive, backed by strong visual identity and subtle storytelling woven into maps, voice lines, and interactions. It creates an emotional connection rarely seen in multiplayer shooters.Matches are fast-paced but rarely chaotic in a frustrating way. There’s a constant sense of momentum, with team fights that can turn in seconds thanks to well-timed ultimates or smart positioning. Every victory feels earned, and every loss pushes you to improve.Blizzard’s attention to detail is evident everywhere from map design to sound cues making the experience consistently engaging. Combined with its vibrant art style and strong competitive foundation, Overwatch sets a benchmark for the genre.Even years after release, it remains one of the most refined and enjoyable multiplayer experiences available. It’s not just a great game it’s a defining one.

author: Booggers
quote: It’s not a game, it’s a marketplace. Fortnite used to feel like a creative and evolving battle royale, but at this point it resembles more of a storefront wrapped in gameplay than a game enhanced by it. Every match, every menu, every update seems engineered to push skins, collaborations, and limited-time cosmetics rather than meaningful improvements to core **** gameplay itself isn’t bad—it’s still responsive, colorful, and occasionally fun—but it feels increasingly secondary. Weapons, balance changes, and map updates often come across as temporary distractions rather than carefully designed systems. The constant rotation of content creates a sense of instability, where nothing feels lasting or worth mastering.What’s most frustrating is the overwhelming focus on monetization. The game bombards players with crossover events and branded content that dilute its identity. Instead of building its own universe, Fortnite leans heavily on external franchises, turning matches into chaotic advertisements rather than cohesive experiences.Progression systems also feel shallow. Rewards are tied more to grinding battle passes than to skill or achievement, making the experience feel repetitive and transactional. It’s less about playing well and more about playing often.There’s still a solid foundation here, but it’s buried under layers of commercialization. Fortnite isn’t broken—it’s just lost sight of what made it compelling in the first place.

author: Booggers
quote: Well, this isn’t an ‘extraction shooter’; if you think so, you’re way off the mark. The very fact that the game was created using artificial intelligence, doesn’t ban hackers and contains subroutines that record conversations is reprehensible, but I gave this game a 1 because older people finally have a game at their own pace. You don’t need shooting skills, you don’t need to think about what to do because you’ll meet another player who’ll help you  (a textbook extraction shooter). The graphics are generic, not revolutionary; the wipes you can do but don’t have to are pointless (it’s not an extraction shooter, so that’s fine); the robots are cool, but shooting to them isn’t satisfying; shooting at people isn’t satisfying either, because if you knock someone down, you’ll hear crying, not insults directed at your mother; I’m disappointed by this. To sum up, the genre of this game is ‘your first extraction shooter adventures’, i.e. a game where you incubate your balls so you can play a  real extraction shooter

author: Booggers
quote: Finally, a real extraction shooter since Tarkov where you have to have balls. Great, unique, non-generic graphics that really bring this universe to life, awesome gunplay, cool gameplay loop, great characters and world-building, and on top of that, a great community . Unwarranted hatred and a barrage of negative reviews make one thing clear: Damn it, if they don't have the balls for this game, then I have to show that I do.
